chose: claim HOLDING COST is a RUN-LEVEL vector on VerifySection (cost: {totalMs, claims[]}), rewritten whole every run
over: a per-claim ms field on ClaimRecord, alongside the verdict it describes
because: the argument the 'batched' field already settled applies verbatim: mergeClaimRecords' skip-carry branch keeps a PREVIOUS run's verdict when this run only skipped a claim (--fast skipping the executable tier is the common case), so a per-claim ms would ride through that branch and start describing a run that did not happen. A verdict is a verdict; a timing is provenance about the instrument, like commit/dirty. The property is asserted directly in test/verify.test.ts ('REWRITTEN WHOLE: a dropped claim leaves no ghost row').

chose: cost prefers the RUNNER's own per-assertion duration over verify's wall clock, and records WHICH clock answered (msSource: report|wall)
over: wall time around evalClaim for every claim, uniformly
report time only, leaving non-executable claims uncosted
because: on a batch-resolved claim the wall clock times a MAP LOOKUP — the suite already ran once, lazily, and whichever claim happened to trigger it would be charged the whole spawn while the rest read as free. The runner's duration is the only reading that attributes cost to the claim that caused it. Wall time is still the honest (and only) reading for a typecheck, a fetch or a serial runner boot, so both survive — but never blended: a mixed column with no provenance is unreadable, so the source rides per row into status.json.

chose: crossing HEAT is the MAX over the chokepoint's defining files of that file's churn share, and ABSENT (no entry) when unmeasurable
over: the SUM of the defining files' shares
the MEAN over the defining files
zero-filling a symbol with no graph node or no history
because: a symbol can resolve to more than one file (an overload, a re-export, the same name in two places). Summing lets cold twins push a crossing past a share it never had; averaging lets a cold twin HIDE a genuinely hot definition — the failure that matters, since the question heat answers is 'is anyone working near this chokepoint' and one hot definition is a yes. Zero-fill is the same lie the batch report's absent durations would tell: an unmeasurable temperature rendered as cold is a claim nobody measured, so a missing symbol or an empty history yields no entry and the render says '—'. A symbol IN the graph over a real history that was simply never touched is a measured 0, which is a different fact and is kept.

chose: holding-cost findings rank LAST in verify's raise order, behind never-red, warned-kind and refutation
over: interleaving cost with the correctness advisories by severity
because: cost is the weakest signal the harness produces: an expensive claim can be entirely correct, and often the honest answer is that the domain really is that big. The three advisories above it ask whether the RECORD is trustworthy; cost asks about the APPARATUS. Since the raise cap is per run and spent round-robin, the caller's order decides who goes first within a round — putting cost last is what guarantees 'expensive to keep true' never displaces a question about whether something is true at all. Pinned by test/verify.test.ts under a cap of 1.

chose: status.json stores only the TOP-5 of the cost ranking (COST_RECORD_CAP), not every claim's timing
over: a full per-claim timing vector in the record
because: the record exists to be READ — the panel shows the head of it, a jq one-liner wants the expensive tail named. A row per claim would grow status.json by the size of the whole claim set every run to carry a tail nothing displays, and status.json is a tracked file whose diff a human reviews. The console report and the record are both slices of ONE ordering, so the panel can never disagree with the console about what is expensive.

chose: the panel's masthead height became a derived function (mastheadHeight) shared by the renderer and the interactive scroll math
over: leaving the keypress handler's hard-coded '- 3' and letting the energy strip make it wrong by a row
because: the strip is conditional, so the masthead is now 3 rows or 4. renderFrame already derived body height from head.length, but the cursor-visibility math in the keypress loop hard-coded 3 — with the strip present the window and the cursor would have disagreed by one row, which reads as a scrolling bug nobody can reproduce without a cost record. One function, two callers, no arithmetic to keep in sync.

chose: the atlas render normalizes its heat bar across the crossings on the map, while the RECORD stores the raw 0..1 share
over: storing the rendered glyph, or normalizing against an absolute scale
because: a bar is a comparison and the useful comparison is 'which crossing on THIS map is hot' — against an absolute scale every crossing in a calm repo renders as one glyph and the map says nothing. But normalization is a rendering decision, and the panel normalizes over its own top-8 instead, so the stored value has to be the measurement: raw share in, each consumer scales it.

chose: vitest's per-assertion duration may measure IN-WORKER time rather than a share of the pooled run's wall clock, so sum(claims.ms) can exceed or undershoot the suite's actual wall time
couldBe: the durations are honest per-test in-worker measurements, and a worker POOL runs several files concurrently — so the sum counts the same wall seconds once per worker and overshoots by roughly the parallelism
the durations exclude per-file import/collection cost, which on a real suite dominates, so the sum UNDERshoots the wall clock instead
discriminatedBy: run a real vitest suite of N files that each sleep a known amount, time the batch spawn with a wall clock, and compare that measurement against sum(assertion durations) from the same run's JSON report

chose: in-worker per-test time under a concurrent pool: sum(claims.ms) overshoots suite wall time by roughly the pool parallelism
because: RAN THE DISCRIMINATION. A purpose-built vitest 4.1.9 project: 4 test files, one test each, every test sleeping 800ms, run through the same batch command coherence issues (vitest run --reporter=json --outputFile). Measured wall time of the batch spawn: 1.04s. sum(assertion durations) from that same run's report: 3207.7ms — a 3.1x OVERSHOOT, and the report's own per-file startTime values are identical to the millisecond (1785465173847-849), i.e. all four files ran concurrently in the pool. Each duration is a truthful ~800ms in-worker reading; they simply count the same wall seconds once per worker. The instrument is NOT wrong — the durations are real — but they are per-test costs, not shares of a wall clock, and they must never be presented as 'the suite takes this long'. What ships is consistent with that: the report says 'to verify N claim(s) ... per run' and the per-claim rows carry their source, so the number is read as summed per-claim cost. Undershoot (import/collection cost excluded) was NOT observed here, but this suite has trivial imports, so it stays plausible for an import-heavy suite; the overshoot candidate is the one this test settles.

chose: could not dogfood either new instrument on the coherence repo itself
because: coherence carries no *.spec.md and no coherence.config.json of its own, so 'verify --fast' here reports 'claims: 0' (an empty cost vector, correctly below the floor and silent) and 'atlas' reports 'no atlas config — nothing to render'. Both features were instead exercised on a purpose-built vitest project with real git history, which is also what discriminated the duration conjecture: cost printed 3.2s over 5 claims with four 800ms report-sourced rows and one 2ms wall-sourced typecheck; atlas printed 'heat █ 75%' for two crossings defined in a file touched by 3 of 4 considered commits, and the panel drew 'energy  cost 3.2s · top 804ms Dogfood  |  heat ██ mintToken 75%'.

chose: the cost report says '<n>s across N claim(s) — summed per-claim cost … (a pooled runner overlaps some of it)' rather than '<n>s to verify N claims'
over: the shorter 'to verify N claim(s)' wording the first cut shipped
because: the discrimination run for d-fe9ebf1e (resolved) measured a 3.1x gap between the sum of per-assertion durations and the batch spawn's wall clock, because a worker pool counts the same wall seconds once per worker. The first wording reads as 'the tier took this long', which is a claim the instrument cannot support. The number is honest as a SUM OF PER-CLAIM COSTS and is what a ranking needs; the sentence now says exactly that, and the test asserts the qualifier so it cannot be shortened back by accident.
